title: literals and their types, the operators postgres can pick from, pg_cast, and five values stored into an int column

steps.sql: SELECT pg_typeof('1') AS "'1'", pg_typeof(1) AS "1", pg_typeof('1.5') AS "'1.5'"
steps.note: the type of each literal on its own, before any operator touches it.

steps.sql:
SELECT oprleft::regtype AS left_type, oprright::regtype AS right_type, oprresult::regtype AS result_type
FROM pg_operator
WHERE oprname = '+' AND oprkind = 'b' AND oprright = 'integer'::regtype
ORDER BY oprleft::regtype::text
steps.note: every binary + that takes an integer on the right.

steps.sql:
SELECT oprleft::regtype AS left_type, oprright::regtype AS right_type, oprresult::regtype AS result_type
FROM pg_operator
WHERE oprname = '||'
ORDER BY oprleft::regtype::text, oprright::regtype::text
SELECT '1' + 1 AS result, pg_typeof('1' + 1) AS type
steps.note: '1' + 1: the unknown takes integer from the other side.
'1.5' + 1: same operator, so '1.5' has to be read as an integer, and it isn't one.

error.message: invalid input syntax for type integer: "1.5"

steps.sql: SELECT '1' || 1 AS result, pg_typeof('1' || 1) AS type
steps.note: '1' || 1: the unknown becomes text, and text || anynonarray takes the integer.
1 || 1: two integers, and no || takes two integers.

error.message: operator does not exist: integer || integer

steps.sql:
SELECT castsource::regtype AS source, casttarget::regtype AS target, castcontext AS context
FROM pg_cast
WHERE castsource = ANY ('{int2,int4,int8,numeric,float8,date,timestamptz,bool}'::regtype[])
  AND casttarget = ANY ('{int2,int4,int8,numeric,float8,date,timestamptz,bool}'::regtype[])
  AND castsource <> casttarget
ORDER BY array_position('{int2,int4,int8,numeric,float8,date,timestamptz,bool}'::regtype[], castsource),
         array_position('{int2,int4,int8,numeric,float8,date,timestamptz,bool}'::regtype[], casttarget)
steps.note: the casts between eight common types, and the context each one is allowed in.
an int column to store into.

steps.sql: INSERT INTO t (n) VALUES (3.7) RETURNING n
steps.note: 3.7 is a numeric. numeric to integer is an assignment cast, so storing it rounds it.

steps.sql: INSERT INTO t (n) VALUES ('3.7') RETURNING n
steps.note: '3.7' is an unknown literal, read straight as an integer. no numeric in between, so no rounding: it's just not an integer.

error.message: invalid input syntax for type integer: "3.7"

steps.sql: INSERT INTO t (n) VALUES (' 42 ') RETURNING n
steps.note: ' 42 ' is an unknown literal too. integer input skips the spaces around it.

steps.sql: INSERT INTO t (n) VALUES (4000000000) RETURNING n
steps.note: 4000000000 is a bigint. bigint to integer is an assignment cast, and the value doesn't fit.

steps.sql: INSERT INTO t (n) VALUES (true) RETURNING n
steps.note: true is a boolean. boolean to integer is explicit only, so storing it is refused before anything runs.

error.message: column "n" is of type integer but expression is of type boolean
